body_markdown:
Parasympathetic breathing is an informal name for slow, gentle breathing that tips your nervous system toward its "rest and digest" side. The pattern with the best evidence is about six breaths per minute with an exhale longer than the inhale, such as in for 4 seconds and out for 6. It is associated with [higher heart rate variability](https://pure.solent.ac.uk/en/publications/effects-of-voluntary-slow-breathing-on-heart-rate-and-heart-rate-/) and feeling calmer.

That's the short version. The longer one is more useful, because most advice online mixes real physiology with a lot of vagus-nerve hype. Below we pull apart the parts of a breath that seem to do the calming, compare the common patterns, and give you a 30-second script for the moment a feed has wound you up.

## What is parasympathetic breathing? (quick answer)

Parasympathetic breathing is shorthand, not a clinical term, for breathing that is slow and gentle, usually with a longer out-breath. Researchers mostly call it "slow breathing," and [slow breathing is usually defined as 10 or fewer breaths per minute](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6137615/).

Your autonomic nervous system has two branches that work more like a balance than an on-off switch. The sympathetic side gets you ready to act: heart up, muscles primed. The parasympathetic side, carried largely by the vagus nerve, handles recovery: heart slowing, digestion and rest.

The labels matter less than the feeling. A sympathetic lean is what the end of a long scroll often feels like: jaw set, shoulders creeping toward your ears, a low buzz you can't quite name. A parasympathetic lean is the opposite: shoulders drop, the breath settles lower, and your head feels a little roomier.

One thing to clear up early: parasympathetic breathing is not the same as "take a deep breath." A big, forceful gulp of air can do the opposite of what you want. The calming ingredients are slow and gentle, not big.

## How does breathing affect the parasympathetic nervous system?

Breathing affects the parasympathetic nervous system mostly through your heart rhythm. Your heart speeds up slightly as you breathe in and slows as you breathe out, and slow breathing makes that swing larger. This normal rhythm is called respiratory sinus arrhythmia, or RSA.

Here is the plain version of what is going on. As you inhale, the vagus nerve eases off its "brake" on the heart a little, so the heart rate ticks up. As you exhale, the brake comes back on and the heart rate dips. Breathe slowly enough, and those rises and dips get bigger and smoother. A [2018 systematic review of 15 studies in healthy adults](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6137615/) found that slow breathing increased both heart rate variability (HRV) and RSA and was linked to more reported comfort and relaxation, though the authors called the evidence limited and the mood findings were inconsistent across studies.

### What HRV can and cannot tell you

Heart rate variability is the beat-to-beat variation in your heart's timing. Certain HRV measures (often called vagally mediated HRV) reflect how much the parasympathetic system is influencing the heart. That makes HRV a useful proxy, not a direct readout of the vagus nerve, and not a measure of how calm you feel.

The best summary of the evidence is a [2022 meta-analysis of 223 studies](https://pure.solent.ac.uk/en/publications/effects-of-voluntary-slow-breathing-on-heart-rate-and-heart-rate-/), drawn from 1,842 abstracts. It found vagally mediated HRV increased during slow breathing, immediately after a single session, and after multi-session practice. The authors also noted it is low-cost with few adverse effects expected.

### What is still unknown

Exactly why slow breathing shifts mood and relaxation is [still under debate](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6137615/). Heart rhythm, blood pressure reflexes, and even a nasal and smell-related pathway have been proposed. The practical takeaway: breathing nudges the balance gradually over a few breaths. It is a dimmer, not a light switch.

## Which breath features tip you toward rest and digest?

Four features of a breath seem to tip you toward the parasympathetic side: a slower rate, a longer exhale, breathing through the nose, and a soft belly. They are not equally well supported, so here they are in order of evidence strength.

### 1. A slower rate, around six breaths per minute (strongest evidence)

Rate is the main ingredient. Six breaths per minute means one full breath every 10 seconds. Slow breathing in general raised vagally mediated HRV across the [Laborde meta-analysis](https://pure.solent.ac.uk/en/publications/effects-of-voluntary-slow-breathing-on-heart-rate-and-heart-rate-/), and for their "coherent breathing" practice, clinicians Gerbarg and Brown suggest [about 4.5 to 6 cycles per minute suits most adults](https://www.psychiatrictimes.com/special-reports/neurobiology-and-neurophysiology-breath-practices-psychiatric-care).

The most direct comparison comes from a [2025 study of 84 college students](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39864026/): breathing at 6 breaths per minute (both a 4-second in, 6-second out version and a 5:5 version) raised HRV more than box breathing or 4-7-8, with small to medium effects.

### 2. An exhale longer than the inhale (supportive, but mixed)

A longer exhale seems to matter most for how relaxed you feel, and it works with a slow rate rather than instead of one. In a [30-person study](https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/inhalationexhalation-ratio-modulates-the-effect-of-slow-breathing/), researchers crossed slow (6 per minute) and faster (12 per minute) breathing with short or long exhales. A longer exhale raised self-reported relaxation and stress reduction. Slowing down alone only raised "positive energy." And the long exhale boosted the high-frequency part of HRV only when people were also breathing at 6 per minute.

This is one small study, so treat the long exhale as a helpful addition, not a magic trick. Gerbarg and Brown describe a [prolonged exhale as increasing vagal influence](https://www.psychiatrictimes.com/special-reports/neurobiology-and-neurophysiology-breath-practices-psychiatric-care), which fits the RSA picture: the exhale is when the heart's brake comes back on.

### 3. Breathing through your nose (early evidence)

Nose breathing has small, early support. In a [randomized crossover study of 20 young adults](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11178300/), five minutes of nasal breathing at rest produced lower diastolic blood pressure than mouth breathing (68 vs 72 mmHg) and a larger high-frequency share of HRV (59% vs 52%). Heart rate and systolic pressure did not differ, and there was no benefit during exercise. It was a proof-of-concept study, so hold it lightly.

There is also a practical upside: a nose is a narrower doorway than a mouth, which makes big gulping breaths a bit harder to take.

### 4. A soft belly (plausible, least tested)

None of the research above tests belly breathing on its own. Think of a soft belly as a habit that makes slow, gentle breathing easier rather than a separate switch. If your stomach is braced (which a tense scroll can do without you noticing), the breath tends to ride up into the chest. Letting the belly move gives the breath somewhere low and quiet to go.

### The thread that ties them together: gentle, not big

Slow breathing should also be small breathing. Even the 6-breaths-per-minute condition in the 2025 study [unexpectedly caused mild over-breathing](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39864026/), likely because people filled the longer counts with bigger breaths. Aim for breaths about the size of a normal one, just stretched out in time.

## Parasympathetic breathing patterns compared: which leans calmest?

For leaning parasympathetic, Calm 4-6 breathing (about six breaths per minute with a longer exhale) has the strongest evidence and is the easiest to use mid-scroll. The physiological sigh is a quick, easy second with the best mood evidence. 4-7-8 and box breathing lean calming but their holds make them harder. Fast or forceful breathing leans the other way.

| Pattern | Timing | Parasympathetic lean (evidence) | Ease mid-scroll | Watch-outs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Calm 4-6 | In 4 s, out 6 s; about 6 breaths/min | Strongest: biggest HRV gains in a head-to-head study | Easy: no holds, nobody notices | Keep breaths small; mild over-breathing reported |
| Physiological (cyclic) sigh | Slow inhale, short top-up inhale, long slow exhale | Moderate: best mood evidence with daily practice; HRV measured, no significant change | Very easy: one to three sighs | Do not force the top-up; stop if lightheaded |
| 4-7-8 | In 4, hold 7, out 8; about 3 breaths/min | Moderate but mixed: heart rate fell in one small study; HRV mixed | Harder: the 7-second hold is long and noticeable | Holds are not for everyone; shorten counts if straining |
| Box breathing | In 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4 | Moderate: raised HRV less than 6 breaths/min | Moderate: holds take focus | No long exhale; skip holds if uncomfortable |
| Fast or forceful (cyclic hyperventilation, kapalabhati, Lion's Breath) | Rapid or forceful breaths | Leans sympathetic (activating) | Not suited | Dizziness; not a calming tool |

### Calm 4-6: the strongest HRV evidence

Breathing in for 4 and out for 6 gives you all the main ingredients at once: a 10-second cycle, a longer exhale, and no holds. In the [84-student comparison](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39864026/), it raised HRV more than box or 4-7-8. Its one watch-out is the same over-breathing note above, so keep it soft. Our [guide to 4-6 breathing](/blog/4-6-breathing-how-to/) covers the pattern in more detail.

### Physiological sigh: the best mood evidence

A cyclic sigh is [a slow inhale, a second short "top-up" inhale, then a slow, full exhale](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947). In a [remote trial of 108 people](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947) practicing about 5 minutes a day for 28 days, only cyclic sighing significantly beat mindfulness meditation on daily positive mood, and its benefit grew with days of practice. Many people find a single sigh brings quick relief, but that "fast" feeling is experience, not something the trial measured in one breath.

### 4-7-8: calming, with a long hold

In a [non-randomized study of 43 young adults](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9277512/), one session of 4-7-8 lowered heart rate (from 71.4 to 66.0 beats per minute in the control group) and systolic blood pressure (109.0 to 104.9 mmHg). But one HRV measure (SDNN) fell 13%, and there was no comparison breathing condition, so the HRV picture is mixed. The 7-second hold is also hard to do quietly on a train.

### Box breathing: steady, but no long exhale

Box breathing (4-4-4-4) slows you to under four breaths a minute, but its exhale is no longer than its inhale, and it [raised HRV less than 6-breaths-per-minute breathing](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39864026/). In the 28-day sighing trial, box breathing did not separate from mindfulness on mood. It is still a good pattern for focus and steadiness; see [how long to do box breathing](/blog/how-long-to-do-box-breathing/) if it is your favorite.

### An honest caveat about all of them

In the 2025 head-to-head study, [no breathing condition meaningfully changed mood or blood pressure](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39864026/) within a single session. Heart-rhythm markers moved; feelings did not shift much in the lab. That does not mean breathing doesn't help, only that one short session in a lab is a modest dose.

## Can you really hack your vagus nerve with breathing?

Not in the way the headlines suggest. Slow breathing reliably shifts heart-rhythm markers linked to vagal activity, and many people feel calmer for it. It does not "switch on" your vagus nerve like a device, and it does not cure anything.

### What the evidence supports

Slow, gentle breathing raises vagally mediated HRV and RSA, during practice and after it. That finding holds across [hundreds of studies](https://pure.solent.ac.uk/en/publications/effects-of-voluntary-slow-breathing-on-heart-rate-and-heart-rate-/). It is a real, measurable physiological shift.

### What it does not show

It does not show that a particular breath "activates" the vagus nerve on command, that breathing works like a vagus nerve stimulation device, or that it treats anxiety, depression or inflammation. Even supportive clinicians describe the evidence base as [small but growing](https://www.psychiatrictimes.com/special-reports/neurobiology-and-neurophysiology-breath-practices-psychiatric-care).

Feeling and markers do not always move together, either. In the 28-day sighing trial, [mood improved with daily cyclic sighing while HRV and resting heart rate did not change significantly](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947) in any group, and state anxiety fell equally in every group, including mindfulness. Meanwhile the 2025 study found the reverse pattern: HRV moved, mood did not.

### How to read the headlines

When you see "this breath resets your nervous system," check four things:

- **Sample size.** The studies above range from 20 to 108 people.
- **Dose.** Many are a single session; effects of weeks of practice may differ.
- **Who was studied.** Mostly healthy young adults, often students.
- **Ties.** The sighing trial was exploratory and retrospectively registered, and one author advised a wearable company; the clinician review's authors have commercial breathwork ties. That does not make the work wrong, but it is worth knowing.

## Why fast or forceful breathing works the other way

Fast or forceful breathing pushes you toward the sympathetic side. Gerbarg and Brown put it plainly: [slow, gentle breathing increases parasympathetic tone, while rapid, forceful breathing is activating and increases sympathetic tone](https://www.psychiatrictimes.com/special-reports/neurobiology-and-neurophysiology-breath-practices-psychiatric-care).

This is where "deep breathing" advice goes sideways. Deep and forceful is not the same as slow and gentle. Several big, fast breaths can leave you tingly and more wired, not less.

Activating breathwork has its place, for example when you want energy before exercise and you are somewhere safe to sit or lie down. It is the wrong tool when a feed has already revved you up. Doing breath-of-fire after 20 minutes of comment sections is a bit like fixing a loud room by turning up the music.

## How to do parasympathetic breathing: Calm 4-6 step by step

If you want one way to activate the parasympathetic nervous system with your breath, use Calm 4-6: in through the nose for 4 seconds, out for 6, about six breaths per minute. Here is how.

1. **Settle your body.** Sit or stand however you are. Unclench your jaw and let your shoulders drop.
2. **Soften your belly.** Let it move outward a little as you breathe in, instead of holding it tight.
3. **Breathe in through your nose for 4 seconds.** A normal-sized breath, not a big one.
4. **Breathe out for 6 seconds.** Through your nose, or through softly pursed lips as if cooling a drink. Let the exhale be slow and unhurried, not pushed.
5. **Repeat.** Three breaths takes about 30 seconds. Five to ten breaths is a fuller reset.

A free [Calm 4-6 breathing timer](/tools/calm-breathing-4-6/) can pace the counts for you if counting in your head feels like one more task.

### The physiological sigh, step by step

1. Breathe in slowly through your nose until your lungs feel mostly full.
2. Take a second, short "top-up" inhale through your nose.
3. Breathe out slowly and fully through your mouth, longer than both inhales together.
4. Do one to three sighs, then return to easy breathing.

The [physiological sigh timer](/tools/physiological-sigh/) walks you through it.

### Common mistakes

- **Breathing too big.** The most common one. Slow does not mean huge. If you feel airy or tingly, make each breath smaller.
- **Forcing holds or counts.** In the 28-day breathing trial, box-breathing participants were told to [shorten the phases if they had to strain](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9873947). Try 3 in and 5 out if 4-6 feels like work.
- **Breathing calmly with a clenched body.** A tight jaw and lifted shoulders cancel out a lot of the felt benefit. Check them on each exhale.
- **Grading yourself.** You don't need to feel a dramatic shift. The aim is a nudge.

## A 30-second nervous system reset for mid-scroll

The best time to use parasympathetic breathing is the moment you notice the feed has wound you up, not some ideal practice slot later. Three slow breaths, about 30 seconds, is enough to start bringing you back down.

You know the moment. You opened the app to check one thing, and now your jaw is tight, your thumb is still moving, and you feel vaguely wired. That is not a character flaw. Feeds are built to keep you reacting, and your body is responding the way bodies do. (If you want the why, we cover it in [why scrolling can make you anxious](/blog/why-does-scrolling-make-me-anxious/).)

### Script A: three Calm 4-6 breaths (about 30 seconds)

1. Look up from the screen, or set the phone face down.
2. In through your nose for 4. Out for 6. Unclench your jaw.
3. In for 4. Out for 6. Drop your shoulders.
4. In for 4. Out for 6. Let your belly go soft.
5. Notice one thing in the room that is not on a screen.

### Script B: sigh first, then slow

1. One physiological sigh: slow inhale, short top-up, long exhale.
2. A second sigh if the first felt good.
3. Two Calm 4-6 breaths to settle the rhythm.

For more on that wound-up, overstimulated feeling and how to come down from it, see [nervous system overload from your phone](/blog/nervous-system-overload-from-phone/).

This mid-scroll moment is exactly what we built DeRot for. DeRot pauses your apps while you reset with a few calming breaths, so the wired feeling has a chance to fade before you decide whether to keep going. It is coming soon to iOS; until then, the free timers above do the same breathing.

## Safety: lightheadedness, breath holds, and when to get help

Parasympathetic breathing is low-risk for most people, and [few adverse effects are expected](https://pure.solent.ac.uk/en/publications/effects-of-voluntary-slow-breathing-on-heart-rate-and-heart-rate-/). A few sensible limits still apply.

- **Stop if you feel dizzy, tingly, or airy.** Go back to normal breathing. This usually means the breaths got too big, which can happen [even at 6 breaths per minute](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39864026/). Slow should also be gentle.
- **Breath holds and fast breathing are not for everyone.** If you are pregnant, have a heart or lung condition, or have a history of fainting or panic attacks, skip the holds in 4-7-8 and box breathing, avoid fast techniques, and check with your doctor.
- **Asthma.** In severe, symptomatic asthma, [slow breathing may narrow the airways](https://www.psychiatrictimes.com/special-reports/neurobiology-and-neurophysiology-breath-practices-psychiatric-care). Stop if your breathing feels tight.
- **Lithium.** Rapid breath practices [can lower lithium levels](https://www.psychiatrictimes.com/special-reports/neurobiology-and-neurophysiology-breath-practices-psychiatric-care). If you take lithium, talk to your prescriber before trying them.
- **Location.** Never do fast or forceful breathing, or long holds, while driving, in water, or anywhere fainting would be dangerous.

Breathing can help you feel calmer. It does not treat anxiety, panic disorder, insomnia, or high blood pressure. If anxiety, sleep problems, or distress persist, talk to a doctor or mental health professional. If you are in crisis, contact local emergency services, or in the US call or text 988.

faqs.question: What breathing pattern activates the parasympathetic nervous system fastest?
faqs.answer: No study has timed this breath by breath, but slow breathing at about six breaths per minute with a longer exhale (in 4, out 6) has the strongest evidence for raising heart rate variability, and the effect shows up during the breathing itself. A physiological sigh is the quickest pattern to do, often one to three breaths. Fast or forceful breathing works the other way and is activating.

faqs.question: How do I know my parasympathetic system is activated?
faqs.answer: You usually can't feel a switch flip, because there isn't one. Common signs of a shift toward rest are shoulders dropping, a looser jaw, a slower and lower breath, and a quieter head. Wearables can show heart rate variability, which reflects parasympathetic influence on the heart, but HRV and how calm you feel don't always move together, so trust the felt change too.

faqs.question: How many breaths until the parasympathetic system kicks in?
faqs.answer: There is no fixed number. Your heart rate already slows slightly on every exhale, and research shows heart rate variability rises during slow breathing, not only afterward. In practice, three slow breaths (about 30 seconds) is a reasonable first dose, and five to ten breaths gives a fuller reset. Think of it as a gradual nudge rather than a switch.

faqs.question: Why do I feel dizzy doing breathing exercises?
faqs.answer: Dizziness or tingling usually means you are over-breathing: taking breaths that are too big or too forceful, which shifts your blood carbon dioxide. Even slow 6-breaths-per-minute breathing caused mild over-breathing in one study. Stop, return to normal breathing, and next time make each breath smaller and softer. If dizziness persists or you faint, check in with a doctor.

faqs.question: Is 4-7-8 or box breathing better for calming down?
faqs.answer: Neither has a clear edge over the other, and both raised heart rate variability less than slow 6-breaths-per-minute breathing in a 2025 comparison of 84 students. 4-7-8 has a longer exhale but a demanding 7-second hold; box breathing is steadier but has no long exhale. If holds feel uncomfortable, Calm 4-6 breathing gives you the calming ingredients without them.

faqs.question: Is deep breathing the same as parasympathetic breathing?
faqs.answer: Not quite. Parasympathetic breathing is about slow and gentle breaths, ideally with a longer exhale. "Deep breathing" often turns into big, forceful breaths, and rapid or forceful breathing is activating rather than calming. A breath about the size of a normal one, stretched out over 10 seconds, leans more toward rest and digest than a huge gulp of air.

howto_steps: Unclench your jaw, drop your shoulders, and look away from the screen.
Let your belly soften so it can move as you breathe.
Breathe in gently through your nose for 4 seconds, a normal-sized breath.
Breathe out slowly for 6 seconds through your nose or softly pursed lips.
Repeat for three breaths (about 30 seconds) or up to ten for a fuller reset.
If you feel dizzy or strained, make breaths smaller or shorten to 3 in and 5 out, and stop if needed.
